transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26 15:00 UTC — Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Jin (MistralTech ML Platform), Priya (Data Eng), Omar (Security), Lina (PM)

Summary: Quick intro, then deep into workload signature, then bench plan and logistics.

[00:00] Evan (Redwood AE): okay good afternoon everyone thanks for joining we uh we appreciate the time today um quick agenda we'll do intros then go into the traffic matrix you folks sent over, then outline the bench criteria and timelines, and end with next steps, sound good?
[00:18] Jin (MistralTech): yeah that's great, thanks. we wanna make sure the pilot actually mirrors our production spikes so uh tail latency is the main gating criteria for prod rollout.
[00:28] Samira (Redwood SE): perfect, Samira here, i'll drive the technical bits — i'll ask about QPS, concurrency, and token mixes and then propose a replay and synthetic shim.
[00:38] Priya (MistralTech): i'm mostly focused on the data side — we'll provide anonymized request samples, but don't expect everything to be perfect, there are user sessions and background system prompts, and the output lengths vary a lot.
[00:50] Evan: quick housekeeping, we'll need a small window for a benchmark run — typical approach: synthetic replay + live-like burst windows + some uniform steady-state. we target P95 and P99 tails for the KPIs, and also track cost per 1k tokens.
[01:12] Lina (MistralTech): can you clarify what you mean by "burst"? our traffic has frequent microbursts from chat sessions, sometimes 200 QPS for 20s then back down.
[01:26] Samira: yeah that's common — we model microbursts as an episodic spike in QPS with a heavier tail on request latency due to KV cache coldness. we typically run a few 20s spikes at 2-3x baseline in the bench. so if your baseline is 60 QPS then we do peaks at ~180 QPS.
[01:42] Jin: baseline is about 55 QPS average during business hours, with 95th minute spiky periods hitting ~210 QPS for 10-30s. concurrency per model worker is tricky because we do both streaming and non-streaming responses.
[01:57] Samira: okay streaming introduces more connection-level memory usage and kv cache growth — in our runtime that affects effective concurrency more than raw QPS. are you doing streaming for most user interactions or only a subset?
[02:10] Priya: about 60% of interactions are streamable — short assistants (like tips) stream, longer multi-turn synopsis don't. output token distribution is bimodal: many very short (<30 tokens) and a long tail of >400 tokens for summarization.
[02:27] Omar (MistralTech): security note — we will need VPC peering for the private pilot and SOC2 artifacts, also KMS for key usage. is Redwood able to run the pilot in our VPC or do you want to run in hosted with VPN?
[02:41] Evan: both are options; for the initial bench we can run hosted but with strict logging and ephemeral keys, or use Redwood Private in a customer VPC — if you want on-prem style controls we can set up VPC peering and bring customer-managed KMS. for the pilot timeline maybe easier to start hosted for speed, then switch to VPC for final validation.
[03:03] Lina: timeline preference is we want a proof within 2 weeks — realistic?
[03:09] Samira: two weeks is tight but possible if you can get the 7-day sample quickly and confirm bench windows and SSO/VPC constraints; bench runs themselves take a day to configure and a couple hours to execute per model variant.
[03:25] Jin: model variants — we run two families in prod, one smaller low-latency model for quick replies and a larger one for deep summarization. we'd like to test both. can you support auto-fallback between variants for capacity constraints?
[03:39] Samira: yes, runtime supports routing policies and fallback. for the bench we'll test each model variant individually and then a mixed workload with routing rules so we can measure end-to-end behavior and cost.
[03:53] Evan: let's define success criteria candidate proposals: 1) P95 < 150ms for the short model on steady-state, P99 < 300ms; 2) for the large model P95 < 450ms P99 < 800ms; 3) error rate < 0.5% and tail SLA breach < 0.1% over a 24h simulated window. also cost per 1k tokens < target (customer to provide target).
[04:19] Priya: those P95 numbers for short model look aggressive — our current infra P95 is ~120ms but that's with heavy caching and bespoke optimizations. important to know how batching and quantization will change quality and latency.
[04:35] Samira: right — there's a tradeoff. we'll run profiles with quantized replicas vs full precision. we'll capture quality regressions via a small eval set you provide — simple nlg metrics plus 30 human checks for the long-form summarization.
[04:52] Lina: about telemetry — what traces will you collect? we need request-level token counts, KV hit rates, per-token latency breakdown, and top failure modes.
[05:03] Samira: we'll provide token-level breakdown, per-request latency histogram, resource utilization per GPU, and KV cache hit ratio. we sometimes see the transcription of KV cache as "K V cash" in our exports — ha — but you'll get the raw metrics.
[05:20] Omar: also need audit logs for calls, and retention policy — we keep logs for 90 days internally, can Redwood match that for the pilot?
[05:29] Evan: we can keep logs for the pilot at the agreed retention; if running in your VPC you keep the logs. for hosted we can retain 90 days in a secure bucket and share access.
[05:40] Speaker 1: [inaudible]
[05:44] Samira: back to workload shape — we want the sample dump: request timestamp, input token count, output token count, model variant used, and any session id or user bucket id if available. that allows us to synthesize burst correlations and session affinity.
[06:02] Jin: we can emit that, but need to anonymize user ids. we'll map sessions to pseudo-ids.
[06:08] Priya: one nuance: retry patterns — clients sometimes retry after 500s aggressively; that can create apparent higher QPS. we want the bench to reflect production retry backoff.
[06:21] Samira: good call — include retries and think-time distributions, we'll model exponential backoff and a small percentage of runaway retries.
[06:30] Evan: for bench design i'll propose three stages: 1) microbench single model steady-state to establish baseline tokens/sec and latencies, 2) burst windows simulating your 10-30s spikes across mixed traffic, 3) long-run stability 2h to detect memory leaks and tail drift.
[06:48] Lina: do you need us to run any client-side instrumentation? we can add additional headers with trace ids.
[06:55] Samira: yes please — x-request-id and sampling for traces helps. for streaming tests we also need to open long-lived connections.
[07:04] Jin: about concurrency mapping — we want a mapping to real worker slots. can you show how QPS and concurrency translate to GPU counts?
[07:12] Samira: absolutely — we'll run throughput profiling with your token distribution to build a QPS vs GPU chart. because response length varies, we model tokens-per-second rather than just QPS; two workloads with same QPS but longer outputs create much higher token/sec and memory pressure.
[07:32] Priya: our output token mean is 72 but median is 18 and median for the long-form actually 320. so skewed.
[07:40] Samira: perfect that's exactly the kind of skew we need. please include a histogram (bins: 0-20,21-50,51-150,151-400,400+).
[07:51] Evan: i'll capture that in the action items.
[07:55] Lina: can we talk about cost KPIs? we want a runway number so product can evaluate tradeoffs — e.g. cost per active user per month or cost per 1k tokens.
[08:06] Samira: we will report cost per 1k tokens for each model variant and an overall blended cost based on the traffic matrix. we'll also surface cost delta for enabling caching or quantization.
[08:18] Omar: security again — for VPC pilot can you list required firewall rules? we prefer a minimal set.
[08:25] Samira: yes, minimal egress to Redwood control plane for orchestration (TLS only), or zero if you run Redwood Private with the control plane in your network. we'll send a firewall appendix.
[08:36] Jin: when you say "prefix/KV cache" in docs, i've seen mention of prefix caching and KV separately — could you clarify both?
[08:45] Samira: yeah sorry the doc text is sometimes terse — prefix cache is caching repeated prompt prefixes across requests (useful for chatbots with stable system prompts), KV cache is the autoregressive key-value cache used during decoding for performance. both impact memory and cold-start behavior differently. we'll include a short primer in the harness README.
[09:05] Evan: timeline recheck: Samira shares harness by Mon (2026-03-29). Jin provides sample dump by Fri (2026-04-02). bench slot week of 2026-04-06. Evan shares SOW draft by 2026-03-30.
[09:20] Lina: ok sounds actionable. one more thing — we'll want an objective quality gating for long-form summarization. what's feasible?
[09:28] Samira: feasible: BLEU/ROUGE-ish is noisy for summarization; recommend a small human eval (30 items) plus automated semantic similarity (embedding cosine) thresholds. we'll compute quality drift vs baseline.
[09:41] Priya: that'll work. also capture hallucination rates on that eval set.
[09:46] Speaker 2: [crosstalk]
[09:48] Samira: on bench mechanics, we'll run both model variants in isolation and then the mixed profile with routing rules. important to measure cold-cache vs warm-cache latency; we'll run cold-start tests where we flush KV caches and run a burst.
[10:03] Jin: good. how many repetitions do you typically run for tail stability?
[10:08] Samira: for P99 stability we run at least 5 repeats of the same bench with cold vs warm cache and average plus report variance. for long-run drift we'll run a 2h stability run.
[10:20] Omar: any compliance red flags? we need encryption at rest and in transit, SSO, RBAC — basic security checklist.
[10:28] Evan: yes, all in scope for Redwood Private or enterprise hosted with additional controls. we'll attach SOC2 docs and an outline of our RBAC and SSO flows.
[10:40] Lina: who will be the day-to-day contact?
[10:43] Evan: Samira will be technical lead, Evan AE for commercial and scheduling. Jin will coordinate on the customer side.
[10:51] Speaker 1: [quiet typing noise]
[10:55] Samira: couple of gotchas to flag: 1) synthetic replay must preserve inter-arrival times and retries to match tail behavior, 2) streaming load uses different connection patterns so don't conflate with non-streaming microbench, 3) mixed routing can mask variant-specific tail issues if not instrumented per-model.
[11:20] Jin: noted. for the sample data we'll also include a column for client sdk version — older SDKs have different retry semantics.
[11:29] Priya: also, we have a small percent of multi-turn conversations that last >12 turns; they increase KV size and sometimes cause memory pressure. include a small cohort of those in long-run tests.
[11:43] Samira: yes include heavy sessions at 1-2% of traffic. we'll seed those into the replay.
[11:51] Evan: any other blockers on your side for the two-week target?
[11:56] Jin: only internal approvals for sharing samples; should be fine, but Omar will confirm security constraints.
[12:02] Omar: we'll confirm by Tuesday.
[12:05] Lina: final ask: will Redwood provide a short doc on how to interpret the benchmark CSVs? our PM needs straightforward metrics.
[12:13] Samira: yes, we'll include a README that defines each column, sample dashboards, and how to map QPS/token curves to GPU counts.
[12:23] Evan: recap of action items — Samira harness, Jin sample, Omar compliance checks, Evan SOW and pricing. Next meeting scheduled after samples received to pick bench slot.
[12:36] Lina: thanks all, appreciate it.
[12:39] Jin: thanks, bye.
[12:42] Meeting ends

Notes: transcript has a few label mismatches and audible gaps; some technical nouns sometimes transcribed imperfectly (e.g., KV cache -> K V cash).
